suggest.instructions:
You suggest what the player might say or do next in a scene of a tabletop roleplaying game, the way a good cRPG offers its dialogue choices: a few short lines in the player character's own voice, for a player who'd like a nudge. They can always type anything instead. These are the lines a sharp player at this table might reach for right now.

Write four to six lines, one per line, each starting with its kind and a colon, and nothing else: no heading, no notes, nothing after the last line.
- say: something to say out loud to someone here, as plain speech without quotes. One or two of these.
- do: something to do, in round brackets and the first person, like (I look up at the hoist). One or two.
- try: a risky try or two that would call for a roll, in round brackets, starting (I try to ...), saying how (talking someone round, frightening them, a bluff, sneaking, climbing, a quick hand) and what for. Something that could go wrong, and would cost them if it did.
- leave: a way out of the scene, in round brackets, only when the brief says one can fit and the moment's right.

What makes a good set:
- Each pulls a different open thread: what was just said or shown, someone here and what they're after as far as the player can tell, something they've seen that doesn't add up, a question nobody has answered yet.
- The brief is everything the player knows, and the lines know no more. The question, never the answer: a line can look at, ask about or try something the player has seen or heard ("Is there anyone he's afraid for?"), but never names a person, place or thing the scene hasn't shown them, or supplies what nobody has told them (where someone was, what they saw, what something hides, who someone's family are, what happens next).
- Only the player character's own words and deeds, as "I": never a line for anyone else here to say, never what anyone else does or feels, and never how it turns out.
- What's true now: the people in the brief are the ones here, and what the player carries is theirs already. Nothing for someone who isn't here, nothing they already have, nothing already done or settled.
- Nothing the scene can't offer, nothing the player has just said, and none of the lines offered last time.
- This character's lines: their manner, their strengths and spells, their quirks and their past give one or two lines a colour no one else's would have.
- In the character's own voice, and the table's: dry and wry, in a world that takes itself entirely seriously.
- Short: under twelve words where it can be, since they're read at a glance.

input.content:
# Who they are
Wren Ashdown: a hedge wizard from the fens, with more questions than answers. In game terms: human wizard 3 (Evoker), sage background. Good at: Investigation, Arcana, History, Nature. Spells: Fire Bolt, Light, Ray of Frost, Burning Hands, Magic Missile, Shield, Sleep, Thunderwave, Scorching Ray. Carrying: 2 silver crowns, 6 shillings, 12 pennies, quarterstaff, dagger.

# What they came in knowing
This morning a palace clerk, Wendell Prout, was found hanged behind the Caerwyn granary, and the Watch Captain has already called it suicide. King Aldren, who remembers how Prout took his tea, asked you quietly to 'see he's done right by' and lent you a sergeant of the watch. She's waiting for you in the granary yard. So, by the sound of it, are some children.

# What this scene can't offer (never suggest reaching for these)
- Getting someone to talk to the dead (a séance, a priest who can call up Prout's ghost)
- Fetching more help (other watchmen, the watch surgeon, a coroner, a wizard, a tracking dog, the granary warden)
- A ladder, the granary key or a grown-up's way into the granary
- A royal warrant, or anything in writing from the King
- Reaching anyone at the palace (the Captain, the warden, the King, any official)
- Coming back later (tonight, tomorrow)
- Prout's own notes and papers
- Following anyone's trail out of the yard (footprints, a scent, tracks)
- Answers that would need someone who isn't here (what goes on at court, anyone's business at the palace, anything about the goblin raids on the King's Road)

# The scene as they've seen it (this is all they know of it)

## Who's here now
- Sergeant Agnes Kell
- Cob
- the girl in the shawl (the player hasn't heard their name: call them that)

## The scene so far (the latest last)
GM: Behind the King’s Granary, a small grey-coated clerk turns slowly from the hoist above the shut loft door. A pigeon watches from the beam. Beneath him, a scrawny boy in a man’s waistcoat and enormous black boots lobs gutter stones upward. “Missed him. Cob’s warming up.” On the wall, a sharp-faced girl swears at him and the morning in Common, then Saltmere dock cant.

A woman in a rain cape steps away from the open gate, notebook in hand. “Sergeant Agnes Kell. The Captain calls it suicide. I haven’t written that down.” A stone clangs off the hoist hook.

Wren Ashdown (player): Sergeant, who found him?

GM: Kell gives a small nod. “Morning, investigator. Wendell Prout, under-clerk of the Royal Granary Roll. The porters found him at first light. His satchel was empty; I’ve kept it, and his spectacles.” She glances at the stones, pencil poised. “The Captain calls it suicide. I haven’t written that down.”

Cob pauses just long enough to choose a smaller stone. “Cob’s helping the dead man spin. He don’t mind.” One stone strikes the cobbles near your boots. “And Cob don’t talk to bluebottles.”

The girl on the wall drums her heels. “He jumped. I saw him. Moonlight and everything.” The sky is still a flat grey after the drizzle.

# A way out
No leave line yet: the scene is still young.

# Not again
The player just said: Sergeant, who found him?
Offered last time (none of these again, not even in other words: the player has seen them):
- Sergeant, who found him?
- (I try to coax the boy down off his stones with a penny)

state.held_from_the_player:
How the GM pictures Sergeant Agnes Kell (the player knows only what the scene so far has described): Forties, a rain cape beaded with drizzle, a battered oilcloth notebook and a pencil stub she sharpens with a clasp knife; a truncheon she has never been seen to draw. Stands very still and watches people's hands, and taps her pencil on the notebook when time is being wasted.
Sergeant Agnes Kell is after: To see Prout off that hook as anything but a suicide before the dead-cart comes at noon, without putting a word in her notebook she couldn't swear to; the nearer noon gets, the harder those two pull against each other. To find out whether the King's investigator is worth her notebook. And the granary kids through this without the Mending House, though they won't say a word to a uniform.
Sergeant Agnes Kell fears: A wrong name in her notebook. Prout in the pit by sundown with nobody having looked. The King's investigator turning out to be a bully or a fool.
Sergeant Agnes Kell hides: Shows: she knew Prout by sight, and goes very still at 'false entries' or the Purveyor's office. Torn: she sent him away, by the book. Opens: the page in her hands, or the investigator asking her straight why this one matters to her. First: 'I'd met him.'
Sergeant Agnes Kell hides: Three days ago Prout came to the watch house and asked her, very politely, how a clerk reports 'false entries in the King's rolls', and whether the watch could arrest 'a gentleman of the Purveyor's office'. She told him to take it to the palace, and forgot him until this morning. She tells it once, in her own words, ending 'I should have listened.' Told is told: she doesn't tell it again.
How the GM pictures Cob (the player knows only what the scene so far has described): A scrawny boy of about eleven in a man's waistcoat and a pair of good black clerk's boots three sizes too big, laced round his ankles with string. Gutter stones in both fists, scabbed knuckles, a yellowing bruise on one cheek.
Cob is after: To keep the boots, the first good thing he's ever owned, off anyone who'd take them, the watch included. To see the men who did for Mister Prout get what's coming to them, without them ever finding out Cob was in the loft: he can't have both, and it's eating him. And something to eat.
Cob fears: The men from the loft finding out Cob was there and coming back for him, which they will if his name gets about: in the watch's book (the bluebottles write everything down) or anybody's. Being taken up by the watch and sent to the Mending House. His father. Being called a liar.
Cob hides: Shows: the boots are three sizes too big and he won't take them off, and the left one crackles when he stamps; he stops throwing stones when anyone says 'the loft', and goes white at the hoist creaking. Torn: he liked Mister Prout, and telling means the men find out Cob was there. Opens: believing someone will keep him safe from the men (a real promise: his name kept out of it, nothing to the watch, somewhere they can't reach him, no Mending House), or a kindness he didn't expect from a grown-up; a real fright works too, and costs. First: 'Cob sleeps where Cob likes.'
Cob hides: The boots are Prout's. He and the girl in the shawl pulled them off the body at first light, before the porters came (he stood on her shoulders). He lies first ('found 'em', 'they're Cob's da's') and fights to keep them: they're his, and he won't give them up or sell them. A look is another matter. Coin or food offered as the price of a look gets haggling and boasts, never the look (grown-ups who pay to look at his boots want them off him); a kindness with nothing asked back counts with him; asked politely, the boots staying his, he might let someone look (it could go either way); and for someone he trusts, or a promise that answers his fear (his name kept out of it, nothing to the watch, the men from the loft kept off him), he holds the left one out himself. A yes he's given is a yes: he doesn't take it back.
Cob hides: He was in the loft last night: he sleeps up there, in his 'castle', a nest of sacks and candle-ends behind the stacks, reached through a loose board behind the water butt (child-sized; a grown-up could squeeze through with effort). That's all he'll own to at first, and he goes white saying it.
Cob hides: What he heard, in a frightened rush: a little after the midnight bells a lantern and voices woke him, Mister Prout arguing with two men; then a thump, a choking noise, and the hoist creaking though there were no sacks on it. He hid in his sacks till dawn and has told no one but the girl in the shawl.
Cob hides: Who, only to someone he trusts: Silvertop, the posh cove with the silver-topped cane, the flower smell and a ring with a bit of wheat on it, who comes with the Purveyor's wagons and opens the big doors with his own key; and a big man with a bandaged hand, who said 'Yes, Master'. Silvertop wanted 'the page', and Mister Prout kept saying 'proper channels'.
Cob hides: Two nights ago he watched Mister Prout, by candle, cut a page out of the big chained book on the tally desk and sew something into his boot 'like a sailor', and thought him a cheapskate. He hasn't put that together with the boots on his own feet.
Cob hides: Since then the loft is wrong, and he knows it by heart: a smashed lantern and spilled ink by the tally desk, heel scuffs in the grain dust from the desk to the loft door, the loft door barred, the hoist rope tied off on its cleat with a docker's knot. The big book is still chained to the desk with its page cut out. Cob can't read it, but to anyone who can, the pages either side list grain wagons for the King's Road marked 'lost to goblins', each countersigned 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor'.
Cob hides: He doesn't know it, but the stiff bit in the lining of the left boot, which crackles when he stamps, is a folded page; and the backs of both heels are scraped raw, as if their owner had been dragged.
How the GM pictures the girl in the shawl (the player knows only what the scene so far has described): A sharp-faced girl of thirteen or so perched on top of the yard wall, heels drumming the bricks, shawl knotted at her chest, one fist kept tightly closed.
the girl in the shawl is after: To keep Cob: he's all she's got. To keep the silver crown in her fist, which is the start of their passage downriver. And to get the two of them out of the granary quarter before the gentleman comes back: the longer the questions go on, the harder that is.
the girl in the shawl fears: Being left on her own. The gentleman who paid her. The watch taking Cob away.
the girl in the shawl hides: Shows: one fist kept tightly closed; her eyes keep going to the yard gate; she shuts Cob up whenever he gets near the night. Torn: the crown is their passage downriver, and telling might save Cob or get him killed. Opens: a believable way to keep Cob safe and out of the Mending House, or her lie caught out in front of him. First: 'A gentleman. Paid me to say it.'
the girl in the shawl hides: At first light a gentleman stopped at the yard gate, looked up at the body for a long moment, and gave her a silver crown to tell anyone who asked that she'd seen the clerk jump. The debts were his idea; the moonlight was hers.
the girl in the shawl hides: Who: a good coat, a silver-topped cane, a wheat-ear signet ring and enough lavender water to make your eyes run; the big man with him had a bandaged hand and called him 'Master Sallow'.
the girl in the shawl hides: The crown, stamped on one face with a little wheat-ear, is in her fist. She thinks the picture makes it worth more.
the girl in the shawl hides: When the gentleman had gone, she helped Cob get the boots off the body (he stood on her shoulders).
the girl in the shawl hides: She knows Cob was in the loft last night and heard it happen, and from what he heard (a silver-topped cane, a big man with a bad hand) she has guessed who did it. She's terrified for him.
People whose names the player hasn't heard: Moll (to the player, "the girl in the shawl"); Corporal Abner Tull (to the player, "the corporal"); Big Hobb Mallory (to the player, "the big man with the bandaged hand"); Nan Quill (to the player, "the landlady"); Arlo Quarry (to the player, "the young lighterman with the black eye"); Dilly Sparrow (to the player, "the old bargewoman with the cards"); Saul Tench (to the player, "the old watchman"); Hepzibah Grist (to the player, "the forewoman with the sack-needle"); Mister Lemuel Scrope (to the player, "the clerk in the counting-box"); Master Josiah Sallow (to the player, "the gentleman with the silver-topped cane"); Marshal Garran Holt (to the player, "the Marshal").
Not yet come across: Prout didn't hang himself: he was struck and strangled, then hoisted up for show. (with: the body (cord mark, the blow to the head); Cob's account of the loft; the scraped heels of Prout's boots)
Not yet come across: Prout found grain written off as 'lost to goblins' that turned up at the river warehouses, every wagon countersigned 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor'. (with: the page sewn into Prout's left boot (Cob is wearing the boots); the tally book in the loft)
Not yet come across: A gentleman with a silver-topped cane and a wheat-ear signet ring (Sallow) was in the loft that night. (with: Cob ('Silvertop'); the girl in the shawl, if she cracks)
Out of sight: Prout's good black boots
Out of sight: a folded page sewn into the left boot's lining
Out of sight: a fistful of gutter stones
Out of sight: a silver crown stamped with a wheat-ear
